Main.lean.riemannHypothesis: Apply the reduction from right half-plane nonvanishing for Dirichlet L-functions to the Riemann Hypothesis. The nonvanishing input is `allChi` and the resulting proof is `rhOfAll`.
Main.lean.riemannZeta_eq_zero_re: Let s be a zero of the zeta function distinct from 1 and from the negative even integers. These are the exclusions in `rhOfAll`, which gives real part 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re: Fix a Dirichlet character and a point strictly to the right of the critical line. The assumption on the character or the point excludes the exceptional pair of the principal character and s = 1. Apply `allChi` to obtain nonvanishing.
Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re: Apply the critical-strip component of `claimAll`. It applies to every Dirichlet character and forces the real part of a zero in the open strip to be 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive: Apply `critAll` to the primitive character and the zero in the open critical strip. Its conclusion is that the real part of the zero is 1/2.

Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.allChi: The conclusion is exactly the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem `UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter`. Use that result for the given character and point.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.rhOfAll: The reduction `Formalism.VW.rh_of_every` derives the Riemann Hypothesis from right half-plane nonvanishing for all characters. Supply that nonvanishing result using `allChi`.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.critAll: Fix a primitive character χ and a zero s with 0 < Re(s) < 1. Apply the critical-line criterion `Formalism.VW.critLine` with the nonvanishing theorem `allChi`. The criterion gives Re(s) = 1/2.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.claimAll: The right half-plane claim is `allChi`. Applying `Claim.strip` and `Claim.zeta` to this result gives the critical-strip conclusion for Dirichlet L-functions and the zeta-function conclusion. Combine the three claims.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_span_of_C_pow_mul:
Write C(aᵛ)g = p C(aᵗ) + qXᵇ using membership in the two-generator ideal. For every degree n < b, the last term has coefficient zero. Comparing degree-n coefficients therefore gives aᵛgₙ = aᵗpₙ. Since a is nonzero and v ≤ t, cancel aᵛ to obtain gₙ = a^(t−v)pₙ.

Thus every coefficient of g − p C(a^(t−v)) below degree b vanishes. This difference is divisible by Xᵇ, so g is a linear combination of C(a^(t−v)) and Xᵇ.

Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.gammaFactor_ne_zero: For an even character the factor is Γℝ(s), and for an odd character it is Γℝ(s + 1). Both arguments have positive real part. The real gamma factor is nonzero in that half-plane.
Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.critLine:
A zero strictly to the right of the critical line contradicts the assumed nonvanishing at once. Suppose it lies strictly to the left. The gamma factor at s is nonzero, so the completed L-function also vanishes there. The inverse character is primitive because inversion preserves its conductor. Its functional equation now gives a zero of the completed L-function at 1 − s.

Dividing by the gamma factor transfers that zero to the ordinary L-function of the inverse character. The point 1 − s has real part greater than 1/2 and is distinct from 1, so this again contradicts the assumed nonvanishing. The remaining possibility is Re(s) = 1/2.
Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.rh_of_every: Take the trivial character of modulus 1, whose L-function equals the zeta function. The assumed nonvanishing for all characters therefore excludes zeta zeros with real part greater than 1/2 away from 1. Apply `Formalism.VW.rh_of_right` to obtain the Riemann Hypothesis.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.factor_ne_zero: The prime p exceeds 1, and Re(s) is positive, so the norm of p^(−s) is p^(−Re(s)) < 1. The norm of the character value is at most 1, hence the norm of their product is strictly below 1. The product cannot equal 1, which proves the Euler factor is nonzero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.prim_zero: The change-of-level formula expresses the original L-value as the primitive L-value times a product of Euler factors. Here s is distinct from 1 because Re(s) < 1. Each Euler factor is nonzero by `factor_ne_zero`, since Re(s) > 0. The product can therefore vanish only through the primitive L-value.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.gamma_ne_zero: Distinguish even and odd characters. Their gamma factors are Γℝ(s) and Γℝ(s + 1), respectively. Positive real part of s implies positive real part of both arguments, so the factors are nonzero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.prim_reflect: The gamma factor is nonzero at s, so the zero of the ordinary L-function gives a zero of the completed L-function. The inverse character is primitive by invariance of the conductor under inversion. Its functional equation transfers the completed zero to 1 − s. Since 1 − s is distinct from zero, the expression for the ordinary L-function in terms of the completed one gives the desired zero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.strip: A zero above the critical line in real part contradicts right half-plane nonvanishing. For a zero below the critical line, first pass to the primitive character using the change-of-level formula. Its functional equation gives a zero at 1 − s for the inverse character. The reflected point has real part greater than 1/2 and is distinct from 1 because Re(s) > 0. This contradicts the same nonvanishing hypothesis, leaving Re(s) = 1/2.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeta:
A zero with real part at least 1 contradicts the usual zeta nonvanishing theorem. When the real part lies strictly between 0 and 1, view zeta as the L-function of the character of modulus 1 and apply `strip`.

It remains to consider Re(s) ≤ 0. The value at zero is nonzero. The exclusions on s also ensure Γℝ(s) is nonzero, since its other zeros are the negative even integers. Thus the completed zeta function vanishes at s. Its functional equation transfers the zero to 1 − s, where the ordinary zeta function would then vanish with real part at least 1. This is impossible.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeta_iff: Unfold `Zeta` and `RiemannHypothesis`. They are definitionally equal, so the equivalence is reflexive.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_mem_vRing_iff: By definition, the valuation ring consists of the elements with nonnegative valuation. Applying this definition to x gives the equivalence.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_map_inv: The valuation of an inverse is the negative of the valuation of the original element. Applying this identity and substituting v(x) = n gives v(x⁻¹) = −n.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_isUnit_iff:
If x has an inverse y in the valuation ring, the valuations of x and y are nonnegative and sum to the valuation of 1, which is zero. Thus v(x) = 0.

Conversely, v(x) = 0 implies x ≠ 0 because the valuation of zero is the top element. The inverse has valuation −0 = 0 and belongs to the valuation ring. Together with the inverse identity in the field, this makes x a unit in the valuation ring.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_associated_pow: The equality v(π) = 1 implies π is nonzero and v(πⁿ) = n. Since v(x) = n as well, the ratio x/πⁿ has valuation zero. It belongs to the valuation ring and is a unit there. Multiplying πⁿ by this unit gives x, proving that the elements are associated.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_exists_nat: By discreteness the valuation of the nonzero element x is finite, so it is represented by an integer m. Membership in the valuation ring gives m ≥ 0. Take the natural number represented by m.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_irreducible: An element of valuation 1 is not a unit, since units have valuation zero. If π = ab, the two factors have nonnegative valuations whose sum is 1. Neither valuation can be the top element, and the remaining values are nonnegative integers. One of the two values is therefore zero. The corresponding factor is a unit, proving irreducibility.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_isDiscreteValuationRing: Choose π of valuation 1 using normalized discreteness. It lies in the valuation ring and is irreducible. Every nonzero element has a finite nonnegative integer valuation n and is associated to πⁿ. The criterion that a ring with such a uniformizer and factorization is a discrete valuation ring now applies.

Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/RhOfRi.Formalism.VW.rh_of_right:
Let s be a nontrivial zero distinct from 1. The value of zeta at 0 also excludes s = 0. The assumed nonvanishing rules out Re(s) > 1/2. If Re(s) < 1/2, set t = 1 − s. Then Re(t) > 1/2 and t is distinct from 1, so ζ(t) is nonzero. The functional equation expresses ζ(s) as the product of ζ(t), Γ(t), cos(πt/2), and 2(2π)^(−t). The gamma and power factors are nonzero.

If the cosine vanished, t would equal 2k + 1 for an integer k, giving s = −2k. A negative k contradicts Re(s) < 1/2. The value k = 0 gives s = 0, and a positive k gives an excluded trivial zero. Thus the cosine factor is also nonzero. This contradicts ζ(s) = 0, so Re(s) = 1/2.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter: The row hypothesis supplies the two row entries of the literature interface. Fill its local reciprocity existence entry with `recTExists`. The same row hypothesis gives the window estimate by `vwin_of_row`. Apply `every_character_of_literature_of_vWin` to the interface and the window estimate.

The integral Galois compatibility theorem `galoisLocalGlobalStrong_recParameter` provides the row for the local reciprocity parameter. Use that row in `everyCharacter_of_row` to obtain nonvanishing for every character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/ThetaC.UpperTheory.LiteratureTheorems.every_cha: Obtain the eigenvalue and first-stage results from the literature interface O. The same interface yields agreement of the theta integrals and local matching. Use the geometric and arithmetic results in O, together with the Hilbert–Samuel and bigness estimates, in the top covolume estimate `topCovolSlim2_use_alt_alt`. Supply these inputs, the local reciprocity existence theorem, and the window hypothesis to `every_character_of_theta_integrals_local_matching`.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.Val.pow:
Unpack the normal-form data for a value of x. Each entry of the two characteristic vectors is either zero or one half, so both vectors coincide pointwise with their real-part vectors viewed over ℂ. The power formula for normal forms then gives the transformed data for y and its determinant relation.

Use the transformed data as the witnesses for the value of y. The new constant is cʲ and is nonzero because c is nonzero. Substituting the determinant relation and combining the powers gives the value tʲ.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.isElliptic_cube_sub: Compute the Weierstrass invariants of the model y² = x³ − x and substitute them in the discriminant formula. The discriminant is 64. It is nonzero, hence a unit in ℚ, which is the ellipticity criterion for the model.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.exists_known_rat:
Start with the rational elliptic curve y² = x³ − x. Its elliptic key has genus one and known value equal to the discriminant. Take its gth key power to get genus g. The proposed known value is the gth power of the discriminant.

After extension to ℂ, choose normal-form data for the original elliptic key. The discriminant formula gives its value in this normal form. The key power raises that value to the gth power by `Val.pow`. The base-change comparison and cancellation identify this normal form with the one for the given complex key of genus g, giving the required known value.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.zeta_ne_zero_of_everyCharact: Take the unique character modulo 1. Its L-function is the Riemann zeta function. Apply the assumed nonvanishing to this character and the given point s. The hypothesis s ≠ 1 supplies the required disjunction even for the principal character.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.riemannHypothesis_of_everyCh:
Let s be a nontrivial zero of the zeta function, with s ≠ 1. The right half-plane nonvanishing just proved rules out Re(s) > 1/2. Suppose Re(s) < 1/2. The value ζ(0) = −1/2 gives s ≠ 0. Then 1 − s is distinct from both 0 and 1, and Re(1 − s) > 1/2.

Write ζ(s) as the completed zeta function divided by Γℝ(s). A zero of Γℝ occurs only at 0 or a negative even integer, and both possibilities are excluded here. Hence the completed zeta function vanishes at s. Its functional equation gives the same zero at 1 − s. The quotient formula there gives ζ(1 − s) = 0, contradicting right half-plane nonvanishing. Thus Re(s) = 1/2.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.imprimitive:
Let ψ be the primitive character inducing χ. Primitive nonvanishing gives L(ψ,s) ≠ 0. If χ is nonprincipal, then ψ is nonprincipal, since changing the level of a principal character still gives a principal character. If s ≠ 1 this condition on the character is unnecessary. Thus the hypotheses allow the change-of-level formula for L(χ,s).

That formula multiplies L(ψ,s) by factors 1 − ψ(p)p^(−s). For each prime p in the product, |ψ(p)| ≤ 1 and |p^(−s)| = p^(−Re(s)) < 1, since p > 1 and Re(s) > 1/2. Hence ψ(p)p^(−s) cannot be 1. All factors in the formula are nonzero, so L(χ,s) is nonzero.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.plugWin: Take a witness of the family hypotheses. The Green condition supplies the shape theorem for these families, and applying it to the witness gives TopG. For each primitive character ψ, the window input at ψ gives the required host existence by supplyChi. Use zeroFreeAll_of_topG with these two inputs and window parameter 3/2, which exceeds 1.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.plugAll: First apply plugWin to obtain the zero-free statement for primitive characters. Apply the imprimitive reduction to extend that statement to every Dirichlet character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.hypV_of_cls: Take the eventual threshold x₁ + 1. At each x beyond this threshold and each index i, membership in the character family gives the two conditions defining GChi at the corresponding host. Its second condition is the VVle bound required by HypV.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.eFamC_of_cls: Use the constant 4 and the eventual threshold x₁ + 1. The first condition in GChi gives EAtH at the chosen host. Its scale coordinates are x and ε, by the two scale identities for the family. Substituting these coordinates gives the asserted eventual condition.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeroFreeAll_of_topG: Use the cyclic tied-window nonvanishing theorem with families FamP and the tie relation ChainTied. Its comparison hypotheses are the level bound on family scales and the form-B theorem. For each ψ, feed TopG the host-existence input for GChi ψ and the HypV bound that follows from membership in that class. This gives the exponents, a positive ε cutoff, and the required families. Each family supplies EFamC by eFamC_of_cls, its windows directly from class membership, and the tie data from connectedness. The resulting nonvanishing theorem applies to every primitive character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.supplyChi: Fix ψ and its window input. The admissible-host supply theorem reduces the conclusion to producing an admitted rank datum for each sufficiently large scale with the specified order and character-kernel conditions. For each ε in the required range, choose the threshold from the twisted-character admissibility theorem. After identifying the scale parameter with ε, the scale, order, and host assumptions are exactly those used by that theorem. Its rank datum supplies the input to supplyOfAdm.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.hostOfField: Apply the host construction from field data. It takes two uniform short-norm inputs, shortNorm and smallOne. With those inputs fixed, the construction supplies the constants and, for each admissible field datum in range, a host together with the required sharing estimate.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.supplyOfAdm: The general supply theorem converts admissible rank data and a character window into host existence. Use hostOfField for the field-to-host construction it requires. The resulting hosts satisfy both the cyclic-level EAtH estimate and the VVle bound at the square root of the scale parameter.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.at_of_from: The From relation identifies the ranks of the point with R and identifies the transported host data with those of H. It also identifies the images of the two sets TT in the ambient frame coordinates. The frame coordinate map is injective, so equality of images gives equality of the sets themselves. After these identifications, the defining arguments of G.At at the point are exactly the arguments in the hypothesis on G.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.shapeWin:
Build the closed conditions for the design theorem from the given selections. The real-place tie, mass ratio, and genus mass inputs give the chosen-rank condition and the global link through link_gl. To obtain the divisibility condition, first collect the restriction rows, stable cuts, chosen rows, one-map condition, nonnegative size, admissible twist link, and the two selection conditions. These conditions hold together by closure. For a family satisfying them, wire_sel supplies the row maps when the required N-link is available. Use these maps and the collected conditions to form the bridge rows, then apply linkDIVt_closedK.

For the existence input, intersect the original family class with the requested G-class. Restrict the selection and duty to this intersection. Forgetting the G-condition gives the original twisted and smoothed families, so the closed size and level conditions restrict as well. The existence theorem link_ex now supplies designs in the intersection. Apply topDesWin with those designs, the closed divisibility condition just proved, and the eta, irreducibility, rank, G, S, and global links. The resulting connectedness is that of the requested G-class.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.topDesWin:
Combine the nine closed link conditions into one. Let ε₁ be its positive cutoff and ε₃ the positive cutoff for design existence. For 0 < ε < min(ε₁, ε₃), choose the threshold K given by the combined closed condition. Design existence above K produces a family in 𝒞′, together with its chosen data and size bounds. Map its class membership to 𝒞 to apply the closed conditions and to ℰ for the conclusion.

The ℰ membership gives HypV. Use it with the N-link and the small-level rank equality to obtain divisibility in N. The closed divisibility condition, together with the eta and size inputs, then gives LinkDIVt. Combine this with the rank conditions and the two size estimates to obtain the μ-link. The global link now applies to the G, S, irreducibility, divisibility, and μ-links, producing the tied family required for connectedness.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.GlobalTheory.Fc.of_hyps: Apply the shape theorem to the family and selections carried by the hypothesis record. Pass the S-component of each C-selection. Translate the divisibility rows and the service condition using their equivalences in the shape interface. For the rank rows, retain the existing constants and eventual threshold, and keep the listed fields of the first row together with the second row intact. This gives the row condition in the form required by TopShape. The record and the supplied proofs of V and NR give all remaining inputs, so the theorem yields G.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.GlobalTheory.Fc.shape_of: Fix the four parameters and the shape theorem. Apply of_hyps with the supplied proofs of V and NR and the family hypothesis record to obtain G.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_span_of_X_pow_mul:
Write X^ηg = F C(a) + G X^(b+η), where C(a) is the constant series a. If a = 0, the first term vanishes. Cancel X^η, which is nonzero in the power series domain, to obtain g = G X^b.

For a ≠ 0, rearrange to get F C(a) = X^η(g − G X^b). Its coefficients of degree below η vanish. Each is a times the corresponding coefficient of F, so that coefficient of F vanishes in the domain. Thus F = X^ηF′. Substitute this into the original equality and cancel X^η to obtain g = F′ C(a) + G X^b, which proves the desired ideal membership.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.pow_mem_span_pow_mul: Expand the yth power as u^y π₀^y q^((ℓ−1)y). Since M ≤ y and η ≤ (ℓ−1)y, factor π₀^M from the second factor and q^η from the third. The remaining factor is u^y π₀^(y−M) q^((ℓ−1)y−η). This exhibits membership in the ideal generated by π₀^M q^η.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_cl: For the false orientation, membership in the window requires h−η ≤ u ≤ h−1. The strict inequality u < h−η excludes u from the window. Since u belongs to U, it belongs to the filtered complement ClN.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.t3: The element u lies in the false-orientation complement by mem_cl. Apply residue avoidance to u and k with the given lower and upper bounds on k. In this orientation the residue being tested is h−u.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.tele: Induct on the interval length k. At length zero the interval is empty and both sides equal M(a). For length k+1, add the endpoint a+k to the previous interval. The local relation at that endpoint gives f(a+k) + M(a+k+1) = g(a+k) + M(a+k), with arguments read modulo ℓ. Use this identity to move the new boundary term back to a+k, then apply the induction hypothesis to the old interval.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.q_numerical_identity:
Put d = ℓ−1 > 0. The natural-number quotient H′ / (ℓ−1) is at most H′/d in the reals. Combine it with the rational term in the bound on eW to get H′/d + H′ℓ/d² = H′(2ℓ−1)/d². This is at most H(2ℓ−1)/d² because H′ ≤ H.

If H is positive, H′+1 ≤ 2H, so log base ℓ of H′+1 is at most log base ℓ of 2H. If H = 0, then H′ = 0 and the logarithmic bound with the added 1 holds under Lean’s real logarithm convention. Substitute these bounds, cancel the +1 and −1 from the left side, and use the definition of aR.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.unit_coefficient_power_mod:
The definition of p₁ gives p₁ − uX^ℓ = C(ℓ)ε. Since a−b divides a^y−b^y, write p₁^y = (uX^ℓ)^y + C(ℓ)W for some series W. The coefficient of degree ℓy in (uX^ℓ)^y is the constant coefficient of u raised to y. Thus the coefficient of p₁^y has the required congruence modulo ℓ.

In the local-ring case, the constant coefficient of the unit u is a unit and remains one after taking the yth power. The correction term belongs to the maximal ideal because ℓ does. If the sum belonged to the maximal ideal, subtracting the correction would place that unit in the ideal, a contradiction. The coefficient is therefore a unit.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.truncation_remainder_bound:
Put A = π₀+ℓ. If y = 0, the assumed inequality forces c = 0, so 1 is already a generator. For y ≥ 1, reserve one factor π₀ and expand the remaining factor π₀^(y−1) as (A−ℓ)^(y−1). The term indexed by m contains π₀ A^(m+(ℓ−1)y) and (−ℓ)^(y−1−m), multiplied by a binomial coefficient.

If y−1−m ≥ c, this term is divisible by ℓ^c. Otherwise m ≥ y−c, so m+(ℓ−1)y ≥ ℓy−c ≥ K by the assumed inequality. In this case it is divisible by π₀ A^K. Every term is in the two-generator ideal, and so is their sum.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.truncation_signature_bound:
Put d = ℓ−1. For T ≥ 0, set A = ℓy−T. Multiplying the first general inequality by d reduces it to A ≤ d max(0,A), which holds because d ≥ 1. Thus ℓy/d − max(0,ℓy−T) ≤ T/d. Take T = X and T = η+M. Enlarging these right sides by the stipulated nonnegative amounts gives the first two bounds.

For the third bound set B = dy−X/ℓ. Multiplication by d² rewrites the left side as X + ℓB − d² max(0,B). If B ≤ 0, the correction is nonpositive. If B ≥ 0, it is (ℓ−d²)B, again nonpositive since ℓ ≥ 3. Divide by d² to get the stronger bound X/d², then add the allowed 1.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_erase_union_le: Removing zero from the union gives the union of the two sets with zero removed. The sum over this union plus the sum over the intersection equals the two separate sums. The intersection sum is nonnegative, so it can be dropped on the left.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_Icc_padicValNat_add_factorial_eq: At L = 0 the interval is empty. To increase L by one, add its new upper endpoint m+L+1 to the valuation sum. At the same time the factorial is multiplied by m+L+1. Valuations add under multiplication of these positive integers, so the induction identity is preserved.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sub_one_mul_padicValNat_factorial_le': Use the factorial valuation formula (ℓ−1)vℓ(N!) = N − sℓ(N), where sℓ is the base-ℓ digit sum. Its nonnegativity gives the desired bound.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.padicValNat_factorial_add_le_add_log: Factor (m+L)! as the product of m!, L!, and the binomial coefficient choosing L from m+L. These factors are positive, so their valuations add. The valuation of the binomial coefficient is at most the integer logarithm of m+L by the prime-factorization bound for binomial coefficients. Add this bound to the other two valuations.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_Icc_one_padicValNat_eq_factorial: Take m = 0 in the interval-factorial formula. The initial factorial is 0! = 1 with valuation zero, leaving the valuation of L! as the sum from 1 to L.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.first_sigma_valuation_bound:
Bound the sum on the union by the two interval sums with zero removed. On the first interval, reflect the negative integers and keep the positive ones. Valuation depends only on absolute value, so the two pieces are bounded by the factorial valuations at η−1 and η+a, using natural subtraction for η−1.

The second interval lies entirely below zero because b ≥ 2a+η+1. Reflection gives the interval from m+1 through m+a+S, where m = b−a−1. Its valuation sum is vℓ((m+a+S)!)−vℓ(m!). The binomial coefficient bound gives at most vℓ((a+S)!) + logℓ(m+a+S), with the integer logarithm in this expression.

Apply vℓ(N!) ≤ N/(ℓ−1) to the three factorial terms. Their numerator is at most 2a+2η+S. The integer logarithm is bounded by lam(ℓ,h+η), since m+a+S ≤ b+S ≤ h and the nonzero argument case follows by taking logs of ℓ^logℓ(N) ≤ N. For a zero argument the integer logarithm is zero. Finally lam(ℓ,h+η) is nonnegative, so increasing the logarithmic allowance to twice this quantity gives the stated bound.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_len_add: Use the maps Y/X → Z/X → Z/Y induced by inclusion and quotient. The inclusion is injective because a representative from Y becomes zero exactly when it lies in X. The quotient map is surjective because the same representative in Z can be used in either quotient. Its kernel consists of classes represented by elements of Y, precisely the image of the inclusion. Length additivity for this short exact sequence gives the equality.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_len_le_of_le_sup: Use the map from A/(A∩X) to Z/(Z∩X) induced by inclusion. Given a representative z in Z, write z = a+x with a in A and x in X, using Z ≤ A+X. The class of z is the image of the class of a. The map is surjective, so the target has length at most the source.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_len_le_top: The map A/(A∩P) → M/P sends the class of a to its class in M/P. Every m in M can be written as a+p by the assumption M = A+P, so this map is surjective. Apply the length inequality for a surjection.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.comap_subtype_inf_of_le: An element of A already lies in C by the inclusion A ≤ C. Membership in B∩C on restricting to A is therefore equivalent to membership in B, giving equality of the two restricted submodules.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.column_chain_bound:
Induct on k. At k = 0 the sum is empty, and the terminal quotient represents the whole quotient since F₀ is the full module. For the induction step write U = Fₖ, V = Fₖ₊₁, X = P∩U, and Y = (V+P)∩U. Length additivity decomposes the old terminal term length(U/X) into length(Y/X) and length(U/Y). The latter is the new summand.

Since V ≤ U, the modular law gives Y = V+(P∩U). The map V/(V∩P) → Y/X is surjective by this equality, so length(Y/X) is bounded by the new terminal term. Substitute the two bounds into the induction hypothesis and append the new summand.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_coker_add:
The commutative squares induce maps A/a(A) → B/b(B) → C/c(C). The second map is surjective because g is. If f(x) = b(y), then c(g(y)) = g(f(x)) = 0. Injectivity of c gives g(y) = 0, so y = f(z) by exactness. Then f(x) = f(a(z)), and injectivity of f gives x = a(z). This proves injectivity of the first induced map.

If a class represented by y lies in the kernel of the second map, write g(y) = c(u) and lift u to v in B. Then g(y−b(v)) = 0. Exactness writes y−b(v) as f(z), so the class of y comes from A/a(A). Conversely g f = 0 makes every image class vanish. Length additivity on the resulting short exact sequence gives the formula.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sub_smul_one_injective: Take x in the kernel of q−ℓ·id. Then q(x) = ℓx, and linearity gives q^k(x) = ℓ^k x by induction. At k = n the nilpotence hypothesis gives ℓ^n x = 0. Since ℓ^n is nonzero and the module is torsion-free, x = 0.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_base: Choose a basis of R of cardinality r. In coordinates, the image of −ℓ·id is exactly the vectors whose entries are multiples of ℓ. Each such vector has a preimage by choosing a multiplier for every coordinate and negating it. The quotient is therefore the product of r copies of O/(ℓ). Add their lengths.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_main:
Induct on n. For n = 0, q = 0 and len_base applies. For the step, use the exact sequence ker q → R → im q, where the second map is q with its codomain restricted. The operator on the kernel is zero. The restriction to the image is killed by the preceding power, since every element of the image already has the form q(x). The three operators q−ℓ·id commute with the sequence, and the one on the image is injective by nilpotence and torsion-freeness.

Apply len_coker_add, then apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel and image, which are finite free submodules over the principal ideal domain. Their ranks add to the rank of R, by the quotient–image isomorphism and rank additivity. The two length formulas combine into the claimed one.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_pi_zero_bound: Choose an exponent n with q^n = 0. Then q^(n+1) is zero as well, so len_main applies at n with the given scalar and yields the desired length formula.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.arc_exponential_identity: Because G ≥ 0 and j′ ≤ ell, we have j′G ≤ ell·G. If the maximum is 2σ+2j′G+1, bound it by 2σ+2ell·G+1 and add the prefactor. If the maximum is r+κ, the left side becomes 2r+4σ+2κ. The right side is larger by the nonnegative quantity 2σ+2ell·G+1.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_le_sum_cover: Each i in S belongs to at least one window, so its weight is bounded by the sum of its contributions over all windows. This uses nonnegativity of the weights. Sum over i, interchange the two finite sums, and collect precisely those elements of S lying in each window.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.kappa_window_bound:
The killer-polynomial valuation formula gives nonvanishing and expresses the valuation at 1 as ell plus the sum of 1+ell+vℓ(i) over the nonzero indices i. Let S be those indices. The windows cover S, so counting with weight 1 bounds its size by the sum of their lengths.

Apply the same covering inequality with weight vℓ(i). In each window, the selected indices are nonzero and satisfy |i| ≤ D. The window-sum estimate then gives Lₖ/(ℓ−1) + log base ℓ of D for their valuation sum. Sum the window bounds and add ell and the bound on the constant contribution (1+ell)|S|.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.second_exponent_bound: The proposed right side is nonnegative because ℓ ≥ 2 and all its terms are nonnegative. For the other entry of the maximum, cancel the two terms involving h″ and substitute the upper bound for c′. The terms involving b′ cancel. Now split (b+S+1)/(ℓ−1) into b/(ℓ−1) and (S+1)/(ℓ−1). The identity b/(ℓ−1) = b/(ℓ(ℓ−1)) + b/ℓ cancels the negative b/ℓ. Bound (S+1)/(ℓ−1) by S+1. The resulting bound is at most the claimed right side.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_quotient_le_of_pow_smul:
Let A be the sum of FFs and ℓ^(e′)M. Multiplying the first summand by ℓ^e puts it in J by hypothesis, and the second summand already lies in J and remains there after scaling. Thus ℓ^e annihilates A/(A∩J). The submodule generator bound controls its length by the rank of M times e times the length of O/(ℓ).

Use the sequence A/(A∩J) → M/J → M/(A+J). The first map is injective, and the second is a surjection. Its kernel consists of classes represented by a sum a+j, hence by a alone. This proves exactness and gives length additivity. Finally M/(A+J) is a quotient of M/A and has at most its length. Combine the two bounds.
